segments.say: One of the people who listened most carefully was an American neuroscientist called Robert Provine. In the late twentieth century he did something that sounds almost too simple to count as science. He went out into the world with a notebook and listened to people laughing, in shopping centres, on pavements and in student buildings, writing down what happened just before each laugh.

His results, gathered in his book Laughter: A Scientific Investigation, published in 2000, surprised even him. He and his students recorded about twelve hundred laugh episodes in everyday conversation. For each one, they noted the remark that came just before the laugh. And then they asked a simple question. How many of those remarks were actually funny?

show.what: Notes on everyday laughter in public places

segments.say: The answer was not many. Fewer than one in five of the remarks that came before a laugh were anything like a joke. Most were completely ordinary. Things like, I'll see you later, or, look, it's Andre, or, I hope we all do well. People were laughing constantly, but mostly not at anything funny. Laughter, it seemed, was mainly about something else.

show.title: Remarks before a laugh that were jokes
show.label: in Provine's everyday notes

segments.say: If not jokes, then what? Provine's answer was that laughter is mostly social. It's a signal between people, a way of saying I'm friendly, I'm with you, this is play, we're fine. Jokes are one way to set it off, but they're a small part of the story. Most of the time, we laugh to keep the conversation warm.

He noticed something else, too. In his notes, the person speaking usually laughed more than the person listening. If laughter were only a reaction to humour, you'd expect the audience to do most of it. Instead, speakers laughed at their own ordinary remarks, as if to mark them as friendly, or to invite the listener in.

Provine also noticed where laughter falls. It almost always comes at the end of a phrase or sentence, in the natural pauses, rather than in the middle of a word. He called this the punctuation effect. Laughter seems to wait its turn, slotting itself into the gaps in speech like a comma or a full stop.

show.title: The punctuation effect
items: Laughter comes at the end of phrases
Rarely in the middle of a sentence

segments.say: That makes sense when you think about the body. Laughing and speaking both use the same breath and the same voice box, and they can't easily happen at the same moment. That's part of why Nadia couldn't speak at the table. Her breath had been taken over by laughter, and her words had to wait until it let go.

show.sub: Why you can't talk and laugh

segments.say: So what is a laugh, physically? At its heart, it's a way of breathing out. The muscles around your ribs and belly squeeze in a series of quick pulses, chopping one breath into short pieces. Each piece can come out as a little burst of voice, the familiar ha, ha, ha, or as a breathy snort or a quiet wheeze.

show.cap: What a laugh is made of

segments.say: In 2001, a team led by Jo-Anne Bachorowski recorded students watching funny film clips and analysed more than a thousand bouts of laughter. They found that laughter is wildly varied. Some laughs are song-like and voiced, with a clear pitch. Others are unvoiced: snorts, grunts, and breathy, hissing sounds. There's no single sound that counts as the human laugh.

show.who: Jo-Anne Bachorowski, Moria Smoski and Michael Owren
show.where: Journal of the Acoustical Society of America, 2001
show.what: The acoustic features of human laughter

segments.say: Their recordings included song-like laughs that rose and fell in pitch, snorting laughs through the nose, low grunting laughs, and breathy, almost silent ones. Nadia's own laugh, if we could record it, would probably move between several of these in a single bout, starting with a snort and rising into something more musical.

show.title: Some of the kinds they heard

segments.say: And the kinds were not all received the same way. In a related study published the same year, Bachorowski and Owren found that voiced, song-like laughs tended to draw more positive reactions from listeners than unvoiced snorts and grunts. People rated them as friendlier and wanted to meet the person laughing. The sound of a laugh, not just the fact of it, seems to matter.

A small notebook lying open on a park bench with a pencil beside it, a busy town square softly blurred behind. It's a reminder of how this research began, not with machines, but with a person sitting quietly and listening. Sometimes the most ordinary things in the world only reveal themselves when someone takes the trouble to write them down.

show.cap: A notebook on a park bench

segments.say: A laugh isn't only a sound. The face joins in. The corners of the mouth pull up and back, the cheeks lift, and the muscles around the eyes tighten so that little creases form at the corners. In a strong laugh, the head may tip back, the shoulders shake, and the eyes begin to water, just as Nadia's did.

In very strong laughter, the whole body can be involved. People double over, hold their sides, slap the table, or lean on each other for support. Some, like Nadia, feel their arms and legs go oddly weak. We even have a phrase for it in English: weak with laughter. It's one of those old sayings that turns out to describe something real.

So here's our first, simple answer. A laugh is a special way of breathing out, shaped into sound by the voice, joined by the face and sometimes the whole body. And in everyday life, it's mostly not a response to jokes at all. It's something we do with each other, usually at the end of a perfectly ordinary sentence.

Back at the restaurant, the laughter has finally faded into happy sighs. Nadia wipes her eyes and notices something. If she'd seen the teapot lid fall at home, alone, she might have smiled. She certainly wouldn't have laughed until she cried. So why was it so much funnier with her friends around her? That's where we're going next.
